speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with respect to the situation in Yugoslavia, the government has received official word that a successful coup d'etat took place in that country early this morning. While we are at the moment without further official report, the news received from abroad is to the effect that the government which signed the axis agreement at Vienna has been overthrown, the regency dissolved, and a new government formed under the young King, Peter II. The new government is reported to include representatives of all parties in the kingdom, and to have the support of the army.
According to the news reports from overseas, Mr. Churchill stated in London to-day that it is reasonable to expect that the new government will repudiate the pact signed with the axis powers. Mr. Churchill has undertaken, if the pact is repudiated, that Britain will recognize the new government, and if Yugoslavia is attacked, that the British will give all the aid possible.

subtopic: GREAT BRITAIN-UNITED STATES AGREEMENT AND SUPPLEMENTARY CANADIAN PROTOCOL RESPECTING CERTAIN LEASED AREAS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: GREAT BRITAIN-UNITED STATES AGREEMENT AND SUPPLEMENTARY CANADIAN PROTOCOL RESPECTING CERTAIN LEASED AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have referred from time to time to the fact that since the outbreak of the war Canada has been contributing to the defence of Newfoundland. This has been done' in consultation and cooperation with the United Kingdom and Newfoundland. Its purpose has been that of assistance in the common cause, and our own immediate and direct protection.
The defence of Newfoundland has also been a subject of consideration by the permanent joint board on defence, which has made certain specific recommendations to the governments of Canada and the United States following meetings in which representatives of the government of Newfoundland participated.
It will be recalled that under the terms of the agreement reached between the United Kingdom and the United States, and announced on September 3 last, the United States was given the right to establish defence facilities in Newfoundland.
During recent weeks, representatives of these two governments have been meeting in London for the purpose of preparing a formal agreement setting forth the conditions upon which the United States is to enjoy possession for ninety-nine years of certain leased areas in Newfoundland and in certain British colonial possessions in this hemisphere. Except as they affect the situation in Newfoundland, the Canadian government has not a direct interest in the terms of this agreement. In view, however, of the responsibilities which Canada has accepted in Newfoundland, we have kept closely in touch with the London discussions. At Canada's suggestion the general agreement between the United Kingdom and the United States has been supplemented by a protocol of which Canada is also a signatory, and which clarifies the rather complicated situation in Newfoundland.
The genera! agreement between the United Kingdom and the United States was made public to-day. In the supplementary protocol to which I have referred the signatories recognize that the defence of Newfoundland is an integral feature of the Canadian scheme of
(Mr. Mackenzie Kine.]
defence, and as such is a matter of special concern to the Canadian government, which has, in fact, already assumed certain responsibilities for such defence.
In view of this fact it has been agreed that in all powers which may be exercised and in such actions as may be taken under the leased bases agreement in respect of Newfoundland, Canadian interests in regard to defence will be fully respected.
The protocol also provides that nothing in the agreement shall affect arrangements relative to the defence of Newfoundland already made by the governments of Canada and the United States in pursuance of recommendations submitted to those governments by the Canada-United States permanent joint board on defence; and that in all consultations concerning Newfoundland arising out of the agreement, the Canadian government as well as the government of Newfoundland will have the right to participate.
At a later stage I shall be in a position to table copies of the agreement and also of the protocol.

subtopic: REGULATIONS CONTROLLING THE BUYING OF WILD ANIMALS AND SKINS FROM INDIANS
speechtext:
The house may be interested to know that probably one-third of the Indians at present in Canada live in the northern parts of the various provinces and in the northwest territories. They live mainly by the chase. This bill is to enable the Indian administration to give them further protection in the sale of their fur catch. It has become the practice-indeed it might almost be described as an evil-of irresponsible traders to go back into the more remote regions, by aeroplane or by other means of transport, and offer absurdly low prices to the Indians for their furs, thus reaping from the transaction a very large profit for themselves. As the Indians are thereby deprived of the full revenue which they should receive, they tend to become more and more a charge upon public funds. The purpose of the bill is to authorize the Indian administration to require, where necessary, permits or licences

on the part of traders so that their responsibility may be fixed and their operations kept under control.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of National War Services):
speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: WAR CHARITIES
subsubtopic: RELATIONSHIP OF RED CROSS TO CURRENT UNITED APPEAL FOR AUXILIARY SERVICES
speechtext:
In view of the fact that an answer which I gave to a question asked by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) a few days ago has raised some discussion, I wish to make a further comment upon that answer.
When I was dealing with the estimates of the war services department in the house o>n March 7 last, as recorded at page 1331 of Hansard, the leader of the opposition questioned me regarding the relationship of the Red Cross to the united drive put on for funds for auxiliary services on March 24.
The hon. member asked:
Has it been found that the Red Cross object to this collective drive? There was a good deal of discussion in the press about this at the time it was started. I understand that some officials of the Red Cross have taken the view that they cannot be bound within the limitations or circumscription of one drive because of the peculiar necessities that may arise in connection with their work. Are they in agreement with the principle or are they standing out? I think in justice to them that ought to be made clear.
I replied as follows:
Three or four conferences were held and the discussions that took place were similar to those that take place at any conference of the kind. In the earlier stages you will find some persons putting forth certain arguments and taking a certain position very strongly, and you will find these same persons later on, in a subsequent conference, turning around and taking a position which perhaps those opposed to them at the earlier stage had adopted. It is true that certain arguments were advanced to the effect stated, but I may say that as a result of the conferences held all of the organizations that are going into the drive on March 24 are going in under an agreement finally reached among themselves, and in entering into that agreement they have one hundred per cent support and cooperation of the Red Cross. As the house knows, the Red Cross is an organization that has been built up right across Canada, having a very good reputation and a long period of service, and it is thought wise to allow that organization at least to consider the matter in their own national meetings before making any announcement as to what they think, or anyone else thinks, with respect to what they ought to do. It is considered better to leave it that way. There has been the greatest degree of cooperation among these people in meeting from time to time and discussing one another's problems and trying to come to a common conclusion.
Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury): Will this drive on March 24 cover a definite period of time?
Mr. Gardiner:	It is the only drive to be
made in 1941.
Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury): That answers the question.

War Charities-United Appeal
Mr. Gardiner:	The Red Cross have agreed
that they will not put on another drive in 1941, so that there will be no further drive by that society or any one of the other organizations during the year 1941. The question what is to happen in 1942 will be finally settled among them before the end of the year.
The statement I wish to make with regard to that answer is this.
Some controversy has arisen as to whether this was a correct statement of the facts. speechtext:
Otter WHILE ON PATROL
On the orders of the day:
Hon. ANGUS L. MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence for Naval Services): Hon. members may expect from me some statement as to the loss of one of the ships of the Canadian naval force yesterday with the loss of some nineteen men serving on board that ship.
The ship, as hon. members know from the newspapers, is the Otter. His Majesty's Canadian Ship Otter, was one of fourteen yachts purchased from private owners for conversion into anti-submarine patrol vessels. The conversion of these vessels was an emergency policy designed to provide some measure of protection against submarine raids on the Canadian coast, and to serve as a substitute while Canadian-built corvettes were being completed.
The Otter was built in 1921 as a twin-screw diesel steel yacht. She was 160 feet long, 25 feet beam, with a draft of ten feet. She was built in the United States. Subsequently she was acquired by Mr. P. S. Ross, a Canadian citizen. In June 1940 she was requisitioned by the Royal Canadian Navy. She was converted into a patrol vessel in a Canadian shipyard. The work of conversion included alteration to her accommodation, general overhaul of engines, and installation of armament.
Since October 10, 1940, she has been in service as a patrol vessel on the eastern Canadian coast. In this function she has given entire satisfaction. She has from time to time developed minor defects, as any ship is apt to do, but these have been dealt with as they occurred, and there has never been any suggestion at any time that there were any serious defects in the vessel or in her machinery.
Her complement was 4 officers and 37 ratings. Her commanding officer was Lieutenant Denis A. Mossman, R.C.N.R., a native of Lunenburg, Nova Scotia. Lieutenant Mossman is forty-three years of age, and his experience at sea has been extensive. He holds a master's foreign-going certificate of competency. He was employed by the Canadian National Steamships prior to the war and served in their passenger and cargo steamers in various capacities, from third officer to first officer. His service in the Royal Canadian Navy since entry on January 19, 1940, includes time spent at the Royal Canadian naval barracks in training, and time spent on the Canadina ships Venosta and Arleux (mine-sweepers). He was appointed to 
H.M.C.S. Otter in June, 1940, and given command of that ship, standing by the ship during her conversion and from the date of her commissioning in the service.
Coming to the tragedy itself, the ship left Halifax on March 21 on patrol work. There was no indication of any defect in the ehip or her machinery at that time. At eight o'clock on March 26 when off Sambro near the mouth of Halifax harbour the ship caught fire. Apparently this fire started in the engine room, and spread so rapidly that there never was at any time a chance of effectively fighting it. The ship had to be abandoned, and this was successfully carried out into boats and rafts. The casualties, nineteen in number, are understood to have been chiefly caused by exposure and also by the capsizing of one of the boats alongside one of the rescue vessels. The weather at the time was very rough and cold.
A full inquiry into the causes of this accident would have been undertaken to-day except for the fact that some of the survivors are not yet sufficiently recovered to give evidence. None of the survivors it is hoped will suffer any permanent ill effects from their experience. It is hoped that the inquiry will get under way to-morrow, certainly it will be undertaken at the earliest possible day. Until the report of the board of inquiry is in hand it will not be possible for me to make a more explicit statement than this regarding the cause of the fire and the subsequent loss of life.
There remains for me, Mr. Speaker, the melancholy duty of expressing to the relatives of the deceased officers and men the heartfelt sympathy of the Prime Minister, my colleagues in the government, and myself and, I am sure, as well the very deep and real regret of every hon. member of this house.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when this item was brought before the committee some days ago a question was raised as to why it should be brought down in this form, rather than by means of a bill. I think at this time the committee will expect me to state -the reason for adopting the method we have in introducing this matter to the house.
I think it will be admitted by members of the committee that -the details of this vote set out in general terms what would be required to be placed in any bill that might be introduced for a similar purpose. Legislation in the form of a bill could contain only general sections providing, first, for acreage payments on the reduced wheat acreage; second, for the power to pass regulations by order in council to regulate the expenditure of the moneys, and, third, for the employment of those necessary to administer -the plan.
Does the minister suggest that that is as far as the legislation could go?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
That is about as far as legislation providing for similar things in the past has gone. Legislation in relation to matters of this kind in the past has been very similar. But that is not the reason I want to give to the committee for maintaining this principle in connection with the bringing down of this particular vote. Two objections of considerable strength might be advanced to the procedure -being followed, and there are also objections which might be raised to the bringing down of legislation.
One of the objections is the time element. It is now thirteen days since the policy for which this vote is to provide the money was first announced to -the house. It is regrettable that we were required to discuss other matters, probably of more importance, during the intervening time, but the fact remains that thirteen days have gone by. Those thirteen days were most important in relation to the question which has to be discussed, in that crops must be sown within the next two months.

Seeding would be well under way before we could have passed the necessary legislation and the regulations to be based thereon.
In the second place, legislation would have a tendency to perpetuate what is only intended to be a temporary expedient. It has never been contended by the government that the proposals making necessary the expenditure of this amount of money represent a permanent policy. It has never been suggested by those who advocate dealing with the matter as we are that what is necessary is something in the nature of a permanent policy. While it might be possible to stipulate a time limit in any legislation that might be brought down, it would be difficult to estimate how long the legislation would be required. Even with a time limit, the legislation itself would give a greater degree of permanency to the policy than an item in the estimates, with a further vote a year hence if it should be proposed to take the same action again.
The main reasons for proceeding as we are can be stated as follows:
Immediately the funds are voted and the method of administration explained to and accepted by the house, we can proceed to set up the administrative organization which will be necessary to putting the proposal into effect. This is essential to getting the proposal before the farmers in time to permit of their planning their summer's work.
Immediately this vote is passed it will be accompanied by the usual bill accompanying votes which are put through by way of estimates, and later it will be submitted to the senate and be passed and made effective. In addition to that, the regulations to be made under the vote can be drafted by the government.
I noted that the hon. member for Qu'Appelle yesterday suggested that before anything was done in connection with this matter it should first be considered by a special committee of the house. It is not impossible, if the house desires that that should be done, that the regulations, which after all embody the greater part, practically all of what will be done, could be dealt with by a committee. But whether dealt with by a committee or as proposed in this vote, the greater part of the procedure that is to be followed will in any case be set out in the regulations, and the regulations could be fully discussed either in the manner proposed or in committee of the whole house. A discussion of the regulations themselves in a committee would ensure the widest possible dissemination of the information which the farmers desire to have at this time when they are preparing for seeding operations. But I suggest that because of time limitations, and the fact that this is not a permanent policy

but only a temporary measure to see us through this present year in view of the difficulties confronting us, we should proceed in the manner in which we are now proceeding, and just as soon as possible we should make known to the public just what the regulations are, and then have the administration set up for the purpose of putting them into effect.
It has been announced that Mr. J. J. McGurran has already set up the machinery. Will he not know what the regulations are likely to be? What is he doing in that regard?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I was just proceeding to give the committee that very information. I believe that before assenting to this procedure the house will desire to know the form of administration we intend to establish.
It is our intention to set up a central office at Regina which will take charge of the administration both of prairie farm assistance and wheat acreage reduction activities. It is our intention also to open suboffices at both Winnipeg and Edmonton. The administration in Saskatchewan will be directed from the Regina office, the administration in Manitoba from the Winnipeg office, and the administration in Alberta from the Edmonton office.
It is also our intention to ask the provincial municipal associations to take charge of the actual work of receiving applications from farmers before June 1, on forms indicating their 1939 and 1940 acreage of each crop and of summer fallow, and indicating their plans for bringing about a reduction in wheat acreage in 1941 by otherwise cropping or summer fallowing acreage which grew wheat in 1940.
We have already been in conference with the presidents and secretaries of the three provincial municipal organizations, and it is planned that they will use the municipal secretaries where there are organized municipalities, and the provincial officials in unorganized areas, to do the actual work of receiving applications and certifying the statements of applicants. It is our intention to make payments for these services, to the association for central services, and to the municipal councils for local services or to the provincial governments with respect to unorganized areas.
We have already consulted with the different organizations concerned, including representatives of the provincial governments, and have been assured that every service possible will be rendered by them in working out the administration. We intend to provide for the necessary inspection by municipal secretary-treasurers where that is thought necessary. By that type of inspection I mean that if a

Last evening in discussing the amendment which is before the house I concluded my remarks by saying:
The position taken since the beginning of the war is to the effect that before any branch of agriculture receives assistance because we are at war it must be shown (1) that the market which existed for the product of that branch of agriculture has been seriously curtailed by the war; (2) that those engaged in that branch of the industry cannot readily change to any other without lapse of time and unreasonable expense, and (3) that those engaged in that branch of agriculture cannot maintain themselves in agriculture without government assistance.
Earlier in the session, I think it was when my estimates were under discussion previously, the suggestion was made in regard to dealing with certain farm products that the provinces could deal with them to better advantage than the federal government. The question was asked-I believe by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-whether that statement applied to wheat. On that occasion I indicated that to my mind it did not. I Should like to explain to the committee the meaning of the statement which I made at that time. It is associated with the reasons which I put forward last night for giving assistance to agriculture in various parts of Canada.
For example, it cannot be said that the market for Canadian bacon has been reduced by the war. As a matter of fact, we are now shipping more than twice as much bacon weekly to Britain as we shipped before the war began. We cannot, therefore, give a reduction of the market for bacon as a result of the war as a reason for the federal government giving assistance in connection with the marketing of bacon.
So far as the second requirement is concerned, that those engaged in that branch of the industry cannot readily change to any other, of course under the circumstances there would be no necessity for change. Since more than twice the volume of bacon is required that was required at the beginning of the war, there is reason for farmers going into that production rather than going out of it, and farmers have been going in rather than going out.
Then, that those engaged in that branch of agriculture cannot maintain themselves in agriculture without government assistance. There may be some question whether farmers who are producing bacon in certain parts of Canada are able to produce it at a profit. There may be some question whether in any part of Canada farmers are obtaining sufficient at the present time for their hogs to be able to purchase some of the commodities which they have to buy at the prices they have to pay for them. But it seems to me that some proof would have to be shown with regard to this third matter before the federal government would be justified in giving blanket assistance to the bacon industry across Canada.
With regard to dairy products a somewhat similar condition prevails. So far as cheese is concerned, we sent more cheese last year to the British market than we have sent in many years. This year we have contracted to send to Britain double the amount of cheese we were sending five years ago. It cannot be said, therefore, that the coming

of the war has reduced the market for cheese outside Canada, nor can it be said that the coming of the war has reduced the market for
cheese inside Canada.
There are two reasons why we have seen fit to give some assistance to cheese production in spite of the fact that the market has not been restricted. Britain herself desires to have a much greater volume of the product than we are able to give her at the present time. Also, if we are to keep cheese in its proper price relationship to butter without calling on Britain to help, some assistance has to be given to cheese, which is marketed outside of Canada in large volume, whereas butter for the most part is consumed within the country. We have therefore given assistance in connection with cheese to the extent of three-fifths of a cent a pound. In the coming year practically the whole market for butter will be within Canada. When the market for butter ceases to be a domestic one. we have difficulties in marketing it at a price which will cover the cost of production to our farmers. It is only when butter can be marketed within Canada itself in practically the whole volume of its production that we have been able to obtain a price which makes it possible for our farmers to produce it, and in many districts even under those circumstances they are not able to do so.
So far as tobacco is concerned, perhaps it meets the first condition which is laid down. There is not in Britain to-day as great a market for tobacco as there was when the war started, but it would probably be more difficult to meet the other conditions which were laid down as to when products should obtain government assistance.
Coming to apples, which is the last product I wish to compare with wheat, and which compares more nearly with wheat, I draw attention to this fact, that before the war fifty per cent of Canadian apples were going to Great Britain. Of these exports Nova Scotia produced eighty per cent, British Columbia about fifty per cent, and Ontario only a small percentage. It became very evident early in the war that the growers would experience difficulties as regards both their costs of production and their markets. Britain stated immediately she went into the war that she did not desire to take apples. This announcement at once put the problem before producers all across Canada. I wish only to say in this regard that the government of Canada grappled with the problem in September, the very first month of the war. They met the apple growers of Nova Scotia and entered into an agreement with them; they did the same as regards the growers of British Columbia, and they set up conditions across Canada 
which made it difficult for apple growers from other parts of the dominion to compete in certain seasons with the producers in central Canada.
In view of these facts I believe there will be no question in the minds of hon. members, when they take into consideration what I have just said with regard to wheat and other products, as to whether wheat falls into the category outlined by the conditions set last evening.
In the first place, has the market been reduced? The market which existed for the product of that branch of agriculture has been seriously curtailed by the war. I need do no more than state the facts in order to convince this committee that so far as wheat is concerned the market has been greatly curtailed since the coming of the war, and that there is not much possibility, during the next twelve months at least, of a greater market being found for wheat than we have had since the beginning of the war.
The second condition is that those engaged in one branch of the industry cannot readily change to any other without lapse of time and unreasonable expense. I doubt if anyone in the committee would even question that wheat complies with that condition. It is not only difficult for farmers in the wheat-growing area of Canada to change from wheat growing to any other occupation, but in many of those areas it is almost impossible for them to do anything else to advantage but grow wheat. That being so, I do not believe anyone will question that as regards the greatest section of the three western provinces it is most difficult for the farmers to Change from the form of agriculture which they have been following to any other form of agriculture.
Then there is the question whether those engaged in that branch of agriculture can maintain themselves in it without government assistance. It might be a little more difficult to establish the case under that condition; but it is not so difficult as it might seem, when one has before him all the statistics with regard to the matter and at the same time has been listening to the discussions which have been taking place in this house and outside it, relating to agriculture. I believe there is general agreement right across Canada that agriculture is the one national industry which, more than any other, has suffered because of the fact that we are at war.
That goes for every branch of agriculture and not merely for the wheat growing section. It is admitted, as was stated last evening in the house, by publications put out by an organization known as the manufacturers association which, apart from the fact that

That was not the beginning.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Well, that is one of the reasons for our present difficulty. I think it is fairly well known to the committee and to the people of Canada generally that wheat growing is a peculiar part of the agricultural industry. Wheat is a cereal crop which can be successfully grown in its best form only in dry areas. Wheat is the staple food of hundreds of millions of people in the world because of the fact that it can be stored for long periods of time without any great expense. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle thinks the expense of storing it in this country is too high, and I may agree with him in that. But it can be stored more cheaply than any other commodity produced on the farm and for a longer period of time. For that reason it is one of the most useful and serviceable food products in the world, and one that, in war time, can be used to better advantage than any other. Therefore, all other things being equal, war should help it in the long run. In the early stages of this war, however, as in the early stages of the last, wheat is suffering under some handicap on account of the manner in which the war has been conducted and has developed. If France had not been overcome in 1940, it is agreed by all statisticians that anywhere from 100 million to 150 million bushels of wheat would have gone into France.
Not necessarily Canadian wheat.

Some time in January. The recommendations read:
Wheat. In the days that lie ahead, it may be that a measure of adjustment of agricultural production may be found necessary in the great wheat growing areas of the prairie provinces, which may involve the re-appraisal of western agricultural resources so that a balance in agricultural production may be established.
In the meantime, the problem created by heavy surpluses is a very real one for the western wheat grower.
The Canadian federation of agriculture recommends :
(1)	That while an adjustment programme may be found necessary in the future, it is not advisable at the present time to introduce compulsory restriction of acreage seeded to wheat.
(2)	For the coming crop year, we believe that the dominion government, through the wheat board, should undertake to announce the total amount of wheat of which it is prepared to accept delivery. We believe that the amount of wheat which may be delivered by the grower in the crop season of 1941-42 should be based on the estimated amount which the wheat board may he reasonably expected to market during the 1941-42 crop year, including both export and domestic sales. Having established the maximum amount which may be delivered, we recommend that the individual grower's delivery quota should be based on a policy which will preserve to each farm unit an equitable share of such maximum amount in proportion to the past production of the crop district in which it is located.
That is as near as one can get to a word description of what was read into the policy the other day by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon).
(3)	That because of the restricted deliveries and in order to maintain the income of the western farm home, steps should be taken to increase the initial payment for wheat delivered in the crop year of 1941.
Again, there is no definite amount stated; it is an increase in the initial payment and not an increase in price which is asked for.
(4)	That until such time as the price of wheat reaches and is maintained at a level commensurate with the price of those things that enter into the cost of producing wheat, a
Erocessing tax of not less than 50 cents per ushel be placed on all wheat milled for domestic consumption. The revenue from such

Supply-Agriculture-Wheat Acreages
tax to be added to the aggregate price received for the wheat marketed and be available for the purpose of increasing the initial payment to the farmer.
I would point out that while the other recommendation did not state the amount to which the processing tax should be increased, this recommends that it be not less than 50 cents a bushel.
(5)	It is anticipated that at the end of the current crop year, all existing grain storage facilities will be filled. We believe that these surpluses of bread grains may become an important factor in our war effort and that in the meantime they should be regarded as a reserve which will ensure a constant supply of wheat to Great Britain in the event of possible crop failure in the course of the war, and also be available to meet the needs of the people of Europe when the war is won.
(6)	In view of the foregoing, and because we believe that the maintenance of reserve stocks of grain on the farm provides an effective form of crop insurance under existing conditions, we recommend that the dominion government be asked to provide financial assistance to farmers for the construction of adequate farm storage facilities to enable the farmer to adjust his deliveries in accordance with the" system outlined above.
I would say now, so that I may not have to say it later, that in our opinion the time has not yet arrived when we should come to a final conclusion as to whether this proposal should be adopted. The suggestion is that we should encourage the storage of grain upon farms by financing the creation of adequate farm storage. Hon. members will agree with me that if we had a crop like that of 1937, or possibly 1934 or 1933 or 1932 or 1931, we would not be very much concerned about farm storage in western Canada, and particularly if we had a crop like that of 1937. Again, there would be certain areas in which we would not be concerned about farm storage if we had in those areas a crop failure like some of the failures we have had in the last two years, even with a big crop for the whole of Canada. We feel the time has not yet come to give a final decision on the question whether there should be farm storage; that it can better be left until later in the crop year.
Then (7):
It is recommended that the practice inaugurated during the present crop year, of paying farm storage, be continued through the coming crop season, and that the amount of the farm storage accruing due to individual farmers be used to repay any advances made to them which may be made for the purpose of providing additional storage facilities.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce announced the other day that there would be a continuance of the policy of payment for storage upon the farms.
Within the quota?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Within the quota.
Then (8):
Since it is anticipated that practically no elevator storage space will be available at the time of the 1941 harvest, we recommend that the dominion government authorize the Canadian wheat board to make cash advances against that portion of the 1941 crop which the farmer can deliver under the arrangement outlined above during the crop year 1941-42.
Those are the recommendations which were made by the organization which represents farmers across Canada. Alongside those recommendations I have placed the recommendations which were made by the official body which was set up to advise the wheat board and the government on matters of this kind.
I think that with the exception of the definite suggestion that a processing tax be levied and that the initial payment be increased-with nothing definite as to the amount-and with the possible exception of the proposal made in one other section of these recommendations, we have already embodied in the policy which is before the house the greater part of what has been asked for in the resolutions of both bodies.
There is not much left.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
There is a good deal left, perhaps much more than the hon. member thinks there is at the moment.
The fact that neither the Saskatchewan pool in its recommendations, nor the advisory committee in its recommendations, nor the Canadian agricultural federation in its recommendations, was able to insert a price, I think clearly indicates that, while there may have been some sentiment in these organizations in favour of changing the advance provided for in the wheat board act, there was considerable sentiment against it. I venture to say that if we had been able to take delivery of all the wheat, there would have been little, if any, sentiment in favour of a change in the advance payment. I think that applies to western farmers as well as to other people throughout Canada, namely, that if it had been possible to take delivery of all the wheat this coming year there would have been very little agitation anywhere in Canada in favour of an increase in the advance payment.
I should like to point out to the committee, before going on to discuss further the proposals which we have to make in relation to this question, just two things. One of them is that the government's policy has set a maximum delivery of 230 million bushels of wheat for all Canada. That means approximately 222 million bushels of wheat for the three prairie provinces, and at 70 cents a bushel Fort William it means 52 cents a bushel for the average farmer in western

But No. 1 northern would not be the average grade, would it?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No. I am saying that is the top amount which could be secured by the delivery of 230 million bushels of wheat.
No. 3 would be the average grade.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Last year I think it was between No. 2 and No. 1. Sometimes it is very high and sometimes very low.
Is the minister saying that 8115.000.000 is the most that can be looked for by the farmers from the sale of wheat?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: That is the maximum, it would appear, which the farmers will be able to get out of wheat in western Canada in the coming season.
Has the minister the average price for 1939?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The average would be the same. The advance in 1939 was 70 cents, and the average for the whole year was 49 cents, which is a little below grade 2.
I have stated the position to the committee in order to indicate that as compared even with last year the farmers are asked to make a cut from a gross return of 8176,000,000 to a net return to the farmers of not more than $115,000,000.
Where does the minister get the 8176,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: That is the figure in the reports of the statistics branch.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce in his statement indicated that
472.000.000 bushels of wheat would be sold by the end of the crop year.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Sold?
Delivered to the elevator at the end of the crop year ending July 31, 1941. If the minister is going to make a comparison, he should take that figure.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I find on consulting the report that I am out by 82,000,000, because the report shows that the receipts for the prairie provinces from the sale of "farm products, wheat", was 8178,900,000.

I do not wrant to interrupt the minister, but the Minister of Trade and Commerce on March 12, 1941, stated in the house that approximately 472,000,000 bushels would be delivered this crop year; and if the Minister of Agriculture is going to take the figure of 230 million bushels of wheat as the maximum delivery during the crop year ending July 31, 1942, he should take comparative figures based on the 472 million bushels, which would bring in well over S200,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The figure I am taking is the figure of the statistics branch, and I do not want to change that figure. The situation is this, that we are asking this year that the farmer be satisfied with 8115,000,000 from wheat, and we are providing him with sufficient money to make up at least some of the difference between what he would have obtained had he marketed all his wheat and what he is asked to take now.
What percentage would that be?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I stated the other day, $36,000,000 from wheat.
That is the amount you would have to make up?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No; that is the amount we estimate will probably be made up under the proposals I have placed before the house. There are other ways, which do not come under this policy, in which the money can be made up.
The maximum?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Yes, the maximum.
At page 1464 of Hansard of March 12, I placed before the house the agricultural part of the programme which the government desires to have put into effect this year, and associated with that, four proposals for the distribution of funds in the western provinces; and I wish this afternoon to deal with those four sections in order to indicate to the committee some of the things which may be done on the western farms as a result of the proposals made.

Would the minister mind putting on record all the proposals or recommendations which have been made? I believe he has gone as far as the pool. Did the Saskatchewan government not make recommendations? It would be well to have them on the record.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I will probably put
them on, a little later. That introduces some other questions which we may all want to discuss. But they are approximately the same -with this difference, that they do set a price of 85 cents.

I think it would be a good thing to have it on Hansard right at this point.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I think it will get on Hansard. Just at the moment, however, I should like to get along.
The first proposal made was this:
It is our intention, therefore, to make payments of certain sums per acre on all reductions made in wheat sowings in the prairie provinces in 1941 as compared with 1940, provided the farmer does certain specified things with the land.
Since making that proposal to the house, as well as before making it, we have naturally been giving the widest possible study to the whole matter. But since those proposals were made we have had in Ottawa representatives of the three western governments and of the organized municipalities, and I have received from farmers in western Canada a great many letters citing their own situation and asking what effect these regulations would have upon their own farm operations.

Has the
minister had any from Abernethy?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Yes, a resolution from Abernethy and one from Balcarres. As a result of the information gathered, certain facts have been found to exist; probably the farmer members of this house knew before this proposal was made that they existed. There are some instances where farmers last year came to the conclusion, "We are in a war; therefore we should seed very large acreages"; and they did so. Other farmers came to the conclusion, "We are in a war, and therefore we should not seed large acreages" ; and so they seeded last year lower acreages than usual. It just so happens that we have on record acreages of about 85 per cent, 75 per cent complete for two years, and about 85 per cent, 10 per cent of which is not quite complete for the two years, of the farms in the three western provinces. Those records were made up in connection with the administration of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act; so we are proposing that, when regulations are drafted, they include a provision that the forms which are sent out shall provide for the farmer making a statement as to what he did in both years, 1939 and 1940. I am sure that some hon. members will have proposals to make which will bear upon the same matter. We feel that this will have a tendency to average the two sets of individuals, one of whom increased his acreage in 1940 and the other of whom decreased it in 1940.
Then there is another group of individuals who started farming this year for the first time.
I don't know why!

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
They have broken up new land, and some provision will have to be made for that type of individual. I will not take the time of the committee in reciting other categories; no doubt hon. members will refer to some of them as we go along.
Then we say this:
1. If he summer-fallows the reduced wheat acreage or part of it, the government will pay him $4 an acre for the reduced wheat acreage which is black July 1, 1941; payments to be made as soon as possible after July 1, 1941.
Now, "black" is a term which we in western Canada have been accustomed to use from very early days in relation to summer-fallow, but probably it is not a technical way to describe summer-fallow as we know it over a considerable part of western Canada to-day. The proposals and the regulations will be to the effect that the land is being summer-fallowed in a manner which is acknowledged by our various experimental farms in the different sections as being a reasonable kind of agriculture to pursue.
Will inspectors have latitude to say what is summer-fallow and what is not?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No; I do not think the inspectors will determine much of that. I think it will be according to the way the regulations are drafted.
They had a lot of latitude last year.

Suppose that this year there is a reduction of ten million acres by way of summer-fallow over and above the normal summer-fallow, what arrangements will be made in that event for payments on such reduction?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: In that event we would have to make arrangements for payments in the same way we always do under such circumstances. Probably we wTould have to get a warrant. The matter would be provided for; the payments would be made under the regulations, and if additional amounts were required, we would have to get a warrant and bring the matter back to the house.
Have the regulations been drawn yet?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: They are in process of being drawn.
Will they be placed before this house?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I said in the early part of the discussion that it was my intention to place them before this house in some form which would be satisfactory to the house.
. . . payments to be made as soon as possible after July 1, 1941.

This morning I had a recommendation from the government of Alberta to the effect that that date should be August 1 instead of July 1. Consideration will be given, of course, to the recommendation.
2. If he sows the reduced wheat acreage or part of it to coarse grains in the spring or, in the case of rye, in the fall of 1941 on lands not summer-fallowed, the government will pay him $2 an acre in 1941 as soon as possible after proof of sowing is established.

Will flax and peas be
considered as "coarse grains" within the meaning of the act?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We have not yet determined what will be included. We are examining into the position of flax at the present time, and will give an opinion on that later. I believe that, technically speaking, flax is not a "coarse grain." Peas, I think, would be.
Would alfalfa be considered a legume or a coarse grain?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
No. Provision is made for sowing alfalfa, though, later. But the explanation I wish to make is to this effect:
If he sows the reduced wheat acreage or part of it to coarse grains in the spring or, in the case of rye, in the fall of 1941 on lands not summer-fallowed. . . .
It will be known by those who farm on lands in western Cnaada that there are some who sow their rye on summer-fallow and there are others who sow their rye on stubble land. There are some who do not believe in summerfallowing in certain areas, and they let their land lie fallow without cultivation during the early part of the summer. They may sow that land to rye in the fall and collect $2 as a result. That, I think, covers pretty well the explanation in connection with that section.
The next, No. 3, provides:
If he sows a reduced wheat acreage or part of it to grass or clover during 1941, provided the land has not also been sown to coarse grain, or summer-fallowed, the government will pay him $2 an acre as soon as possible after proof of sowing has been established, and an additional $2 an acre if the same land is still seeded down to grass on July 1, 1942.
The intention of that section is to get land seeded to grass in the first place and, in the second place, to keep it seeded to grass for the second year, which is the only reason for seeding it to begin with. This would tend to prevent it from being ploughed up again and put back into wheat the second year.

Suppose a farmer had a volunteer crop of sweet clover. Many of us in Manitoba have been sowing sweet clover for years and the land is practically full of that seed. Suppose a farmer should wish to
	*
let that land produce a sweet clover crop this summer; would that be classed as falling within that section?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I am afraid not, although I should not like to express a definite opinion on the point at this stage. It would not come under this particular section or any section that I have read so far.
A good deal of it will be done in Manitoba. It is done to a certain extent every year.

Why is a distinction made between the man who seeds down with a coarse grain crop and the man who seeds down without? In our section we seed down to clover along with a coarse grain crop, according to the regulation. We do not receive $2 an acre if we seed down with the use of coarse grain.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: There is no difference in the position so far as this year is concerned. That is to say, the man will get $2 if he seeds coarse grain in the spring, and he will get $2 if he seeds grass on stubble in the spring. In certain sections of the west where it is dry, it would be wise to put it in with a nurse crop. In the section in which my hon. friend farms it would not be wise to put it in the nurse crop, so that we do not desire to provide for seed in the nurse crop in that case, because we consider that a good deal would be wasted in certain sections. But in a section where it is the proper thing to seed in the nurse crop, $2 is paid for the nurse and $2 the following year for the grass.
If he sows two crops he gets two returns, provided he has summer-fallowed?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Through the two years, yes. By July, 1942, he would be almost ready to cut a wheat crop on the other land.
The next section, No. 4, provides:
If he sows a reduced wheat acreage or part of it, which is also sown to coarse grain or which is summer-fallowed in 1941 to grass or and clover, or to rye in 1941, the government will pay $2 an acre as soon as possible after July 1, 1942, provided the same land is in grass or and clover or rye on that date.
It will be noted that under that a man can take a summer-fallow on which he drew $4 an acre in the spring and sow it to grass in the fall, as many farmers do. They sow crested wheat grass in the fall. On the other hand, he can sow it to rye, as many farmers do. He will get nothing for sowing rye or crested wheat grass on summer-fallow in the fall of 1941; but if he leaves the rye or crested wheat grass on the land until July 1, 1942, he will

receive $2 an acre for having sown it. This means that if it were summer-fallowed this year, and there were still grass or rye crop on it on July 1 next, in the two years he would have collected by that method, $6.
If he summer-fallowed one year and got $4 and seeded it in the spring as a nurse crop, he would get 84 more; and if he summer-fallowed the next year, would he still get more?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: There is no provision for seeding anything in the second year. That is why I said that I did not wish to place these regulations on the statute books in the form of legislation. It is simply a provision for this season for the carryover of grass or rye into the succeeding year.

Is that only on reduced
wheat acreage?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes, only on reduced wheat acreage. If a man had 100 acres of wheat and reduced his wheat acreage by 40 acres, that is, if he had 100 acres in wheat last year and this year seeded only sixty acres of wheat, and summer-fallowed twenty acres, sowing the other twenty acres to grass or coarse grains, then he would receive 84 an acre on twenty acres and $2 an acre on the other twenty. I think that is all it is necessary for me to say to explain the intentions of the government in making payments to farmers.
Suppose a man did not have any wheat in, last year-and there are several [DOT]-would he come into the picture at all?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: If he had wheat in 1939. We intend to take the two years.
But he loses 1940.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
We intend to take two years and average them, and he would probably have some recognition because of what he had done in 1939. I should not say that we intend to take two years and average them; we are getting information now on which to base the regulations so that they will be fair to all farmers throughout the west. We may decide to take 1939 instead of 1940 because of the fact that the war had not entered into the picture in 1939 when the crop was sown, but we wish to look into all the facts before deciding finally what should be done. Something will be done to take care of such cases.
Mr. "WEIR: Has the point been considered with reference to grass that may have been seeded last fall? On certain lands in Manitoba grass is seeded the fall before, which ordinarily would be seeded in the spring of 1941. That is one class of farmers I have in mind. There is another class of farmers
who are to a large extent using corn as a summer-fallow substitute. They are using larger acreages for summer-fallowing, sowing corn wider apart. They regard it as a method of summer-fallowing rather than as the production of a corn crop. Is consideration being given to that?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I would rather wait until we have the regulations in front of us before discussing too many details. So far as the first case is concerned, the person who farms in that way is taken care of in the proposals. If the proper method of sowing grass seed in that particular area is to sow it in the fall, the farmer will get the advantage of the provision which states that if he does sow it in the fall of this year he will receive $2. We are not paying anything for anything done last year.

In view of the statement the minister has made, taking into account the years 1939 and 1940, the basis would have reference to acreage rather than to the operator? That would be based on the acreage, irrespective of the operator? For instance, there are many tenants who change each year.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes, it would have to be based on the land and what was done with the land the year before, taken into consideration. There will be a great many variations; that is the reason we have to do it by regulation. There might be a father whose son gets married this year and who divides his farm; or a man who sells part of his farm, and it may be found that all the wheat was on the part now in possession of another. There are scores of cases, and the matter must be dealt with by regulation.
Will alfalfa be classed as grass?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: There is no doubt about that. It says "grass or clover."

Would ths minister
amplify what is likely to be the regulation concerning tenants on land? Will the amount be paid to the tenant or the owner?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The present intention, and I think it will be carried into the regulations, is that this proposal will follow a different principle from that of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. Under that act the purpose is to give assistance to people who, because they have a poor crop in a particular year, require help. That is for the purpose of maintaining on the land the people who are on the land. This legislation is for the purpose of giving a larger return to people who are being denied the right to sell their wheat this year.

Will there be provision for dealing with new land, taken in 1939, broken in 1940?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes; there will have to be provision made for that land. It will have to be taken on an average basis or some other such basis.

I desire to say a few words, not on the principle of the proposal but on the procedure proposed to be adopted. I had intended to make my protest with regard to this matter before the minister made his general statement. I shall, however, do so now.
I suggest to the minister that the reason which he gave for bringing down the wheat policy as an estimate is totally inadequate and is not in accordance with the precedents heretofore followed in this house. It is a denial of the principle of responsible government. We are asked to vote money but are not to have any say at all with respect to the manner in which it is to be expended. This house is not a mere debating society. It is the supreme legislative body of the nation, and it is the right and the duty of this house and of parliament to pass in legislative form the policy to be followed and to prescribe the conditions under which that policy shall be placed in effect; not merely to order the issue of a blank cheque to the Department of Agriculture.
Apart from the situation in this chamber, the proposed procedure of merely tacking a policy on to a supplementary estimate or money bill will, under our rules and practice in parliament, preclude the other chamber from dealing with this matter, one of the most important, if not the most important of our domestic problems.
I do not understand why the Prime Minister, who throughout his public life has so frequently declared his belief in the supremacy of parliament, should insist upon this procedure. With all the emphasis and sincerity at my command I appeal to him to turn back to our established and time-tried procedure and to allow this parliament, not the governor in council, to take the necessary legislative action.
What is proposed to be done is not sound policy and procedure. I have said on many 
occasions that, since the war began, we in this house have abdicated our function. This course should not be pursued any further. In a domestic problem like this, parliament should regain some of its supremacy and authority. On a purely domestic issue such as wheat, surely the minister will not deal with it by a mere vote in the estimates.
May I remind the minister and the committee that in 1931 when the crop yield was low, prices low and farm income low, the then government undertook to help the wheat producers by a bonus of five cents a bushel. This was done by way of a bill, not an estimate. Such a course as the latter was not even suggested. The bill as introduced was passed and became chapter 60 of 21-22 George V. 1931. The principle was embodied in the bill, and the supremacy of parliament was recognized.
I turn now to that legislation. It was temporary in its nature, just as this is. It was not a policy that was to continue. This is what it provided for, after the preamble;
1. The governor in council may authorize the payment, out of the consolidated revenue fund, of the sum of five cents for every bushel of wheat grown in the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba in the year 1931, and delivered to any licenced elevator in the western inspection division, commission merchant, track buyer or grain dealer, as defined by the Canada Grain Act.
The governor in council did take authority to make regulations, but I call attention to this very important fact, especially from a legal point of view, that those regulations were confined to regulations of certain specific character. They were to make regulations for:
(a)	the kind, form and terms of the document to be issued on the delivery of wheat to any elevator or over a loading platform;
(b)	determining the person to whom the said sum of five cents per bushel shall be paid and the method of the payment thereof;
(c)	making such arrangements as may be necessary with the Board of Grain Commissioners for Canada or other statutory body for payment of the said sum;
(d)	the keeping of proper books and records by the operator or manager of any country elevator or other person receiving such grain, and the examination and audit of the same;
(e)	preventing fraud, misrepresentation or illegal or improper conduct on the part of any person or persons in any way concerned in the carrying out of the provisions of this act or any regulations made thereunder;
(f)	prescribing penalties to be imposed for breach of the provisions of this act or the regulations made thereunder.
Finally, the act was to expire on July 31, 1932, namely, the end of the then crop year.
To say that this is a temporary measure and, therefore, should be given effect to by a supplementary estimate is, I submit, an absolute non sequitur and is against the pro-

Supply-Agriculture-Wheat Acreages
cedure heretofore adopted in temporary measures of this kind in this house. I suggest to the minister that if he is determined to persist in the policy or procedure now before the committee, this estimate should not be passed until the regulations are brought down and we may know what they are.
I appeal to the private members of this house to insist that this be done, because they are giving to the minister-to this minister-a blank cheque to say how
S35.000.000 may be distributed among the farmers of the three western provinces; and from what we have heard to-day, let me say it is not limited to $35,000,000; it may be double that sum. And it will be paid under a governor general's warrant. If hon. gentlemen did not understand the implication of the minister's language, I suggest that they read it carefully. That $35,000,000, the amount mentioned in the estimate itself, is not the limit of the final bill which the taxpayers of Canada will have to pay, whether or not one approves the principle of this resolution.
Finally, I suggest to the minister that the whole matter should be sent to a special committee, where every party and interest may have an opportunity to be heard and to present their views. There is a wide division of opinion in this country as to the adequacy or otherwise of this policy. Why is it that opportunity is given to only a few to present their views to the government of the day concerning the policy to be adopted? Many others who have not access to the ministry do not have that opportunity.
I remember the time when the principle of setting up a wheat board was discussed-and I shall have something to say about that at a later stage in these proceedings. A new principle was being adopted, a principle which might or might not become permanent government policy. Time has shown that it was the only correct policy; it has come down from that day to this, and is operative to-day. Hon. gentlemen opposite, who were then sitting on this side of the house demanded that the principle of the bill be submitted to a special committee, and that was done. They were opposed to the principle of the bill, but they were afraid to strike. The bill went to a committee, and when it emerged it was greatly improved because it had been so submitted. The principle was sustained, and the democratic method of legislating in respect of the people's money was also sustained.
I say to the minister, to hon. members and to the people of Canada that the method here suggested is wrong. This method is wrong.
What about the committee on agriculture?

There may
be some difference of opinion. I never sat on the committee on agriculture, and I do not know whether it would be the proper body.

It is a much larger
committee.

Probably it is too large; that would probably be an argument against it. I suggest there ought to be a special committee, carefully selected from among the membership in this house, and consisting of hon. members who know most about wheat. They would be the best judges of what Should be done in the circumstances, and what policy should be followed. They would have power to deal particularly with the details of such a policy, and especially they would have information respecting methods of procedure and methods of payment.
What have wre here? Just read the estimate:
To provide for payments on reductions in wheat acreages, under conditions prescribed by the governor in council-
And then it continues:

for administration expenses in connection therewith, and for temporary appointments that may be required notwithstanding anything contained in the Civil Service Act.
In other words, on a purely domestic problem we are being asked to delegate to the governor in council the whole task of legislating on this important proposition. All we are asked to do is to supply the money. That is a direct negation of the principle of responsible government. I appeal to the minister, if he is bound to. proceed in this way, that the whole question be submitted to a special, select committee of the house. I make the further appeal that the procedure he is adopting is not the right one. It is not the way in which parliament has handled this sort of thing before.
I suggest that the method adopted in 1931 was the correct one, and that both branches of parliament should have something to say about this. This is a clever method of preventing hon. gentlemen in the other chamber, gentlemen who know as much about the wheat problem as hon. members in this house know, and who have had a long experience in the business, from having anything to say about how this money shall be expended.
I suggest to the minister that it is not too late to reverse his position. This matter should come to us in the form of a bill; it should be placed in a statute, and the framing of regulations which may be changed at will should not be left to the governor in council. Those regulations may be changed, not once or twice, but from time to time, to

Mr. Chairman, in rising
to make a few remarks in connection with the wheat policy, I desire to refer briefly to some of the statements made yesterday by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) when he suggested that there would be full opportunity on the discussion of this vote to deal with the agricultural problem of the west. It is not my intention to deal at any length with what might be termed the general agricultural problem. I feel quite confident that in connection with the government's record and agricultural policy I can find much for which to commend them and also some things for which they could be criticized. The minister made a further statement with reference to the matter under discussion and left the inference that the matter had not been closed entirely, that after full discussion had been had, the government might decide to make any adjustments or changes which were deemed advisable. I noticed a statement in the press to the effect that the municipal representatives from western Canada had left for their homes yesterday or the day before to prepare

to put this policy into operation. I was much concerned when I read that statement, but I was pleased to note the remarks made yesterday by the minister.
There are two or three matters which came up in the general discussion and which, I believe, have a direct bearing upon this question. It has been said that the production of munitions in Canada has been centred largely in the central provinces. Of course, that is a matter for the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe), and I think it is in good hands. I do not know which province has the largest per capita expenditure on munitions, but the point I wish to make is that this vastly increased programme for the production of munitions has to a certain extent assisted the farmers from one end of Canada to the other. It has created larger markets for beef, pork, butter and poultry products, and all farmers have benefited similarly from this production. In Ontario, however, I do not think we can say that the production of munitions is of great advantage to the farming population, particularly in the areas where the production is taking place. In some instances this production has increased rather than decreased farm problems. It has taken much labour away from the farm and has increased the cost of what labour is still available for that type of work.
A further statement was made with respect to the pay and allowances of our troops being centred in certain portions of Canada. It would be a foolish question to ask, but we could inquire the extent of the pay and allowances being paid to our forces in England. I contend that our forces must be centred where they can do the most effective work, and the matter of pay and allowances is an unimportant item. The country is at war, and our forces are not protecting just the wheat grower or the hog producer; they are protecting the vital interests of all the people in all the provinces across Canada.
During the discussion this afternoon it was said that the wheat question was a war casualty. I do not contend that the wheat problem has not been affected by the war, that is up to a certain point, but it has been affected to a far greater extent by the weather. It is a weather casualty rather than a war casualty. I think I can prove this statement by giving the wheat production for the three-year periods 1935 to 1937 and 1938 to 1940. The production figures are as follows:
Year	Bushels
1935		 264,096,000
1936		 202,000,000
1937		 156,800,000
1938		 336,000.000
1939		 494,000,000
1940		 525,000,000
The total production for the first three-year period was 622,896,000 bushels, and for the second three-year period 1,355,000,000 bushels. If we want to get a true picture of the situation, we should reverse these production figures, putting the production in the latter period into the first. Dealing with this matter, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) said recently that as of July 31, 1941, he expected that we would have a wheat carryover of 575,000,000 bushels. If the production figures were reversed, instead or having a carryover of 23,000,000 bushels on July 31, 1938, we would have had a carryover of
758,000,000 bushels, or 175,000,000 bushels more than we expect to have as of July 31, 1941. I think I am within the bounds of reason when I say that our wheat problem is to a far greater extent affected by weather than it is by war.
I believe that the new wheat policy can be divided into three main divisions. First, there is the proposal to pay $4 an acre for summer-fallow; second, $2 an acre is to be paid for seeding for grass or clover; and, third, $2 an acre is to be paid as a bonus for the production of coarse grains. I shall deal with these in the order in which I have listed them. I do not think I can be accused of ever having been unsympathetic to the problems or needs of western Canada. During the discussions which have occurred previously in this chamber with regard to wheat policies, I contended as vigorously as I could that a limit of 5,000 bushels should be placed upon the amount of grain that any one farmer could deliver to the government at a set price. I have had no reason to retract from that stand. Had we adopted that policy, even as late as the spring of 1940, I contend that our problem to-day would not be as great as it is.
This brings me to the summer-fallow question. I believe that this principle should be applied here. If that is done, then I think we can reach a compromise in which I would agree fully. In order further to illustrate this point, I would refer to the fact that in connection with old age pensions we have placed a limit upon the amount of money that may be taken out of the treasury. An old age pensioner, with a wife to support, can draw the full amount of S20 a month and still have an earning capacity of $250 a year. But the minute his earning capacity increases beyond that $250 the pension is reduced by the amount of that increase. We have adopted here a principle that there must be a limit to the amount of money which can be taken out of the treasury by a single individual. I might enlarge upon that and say that the same principle is applied to those people in receipt of blind pensions.
