I go further and state that the same principle is followed in the payment of dependent's allowance. I know of a woman whose husband is an old age pensioner getting $20 a month, and who had an earning capacity of SI a day in the summer time. She had a son in the army who turned over his assigned pay and dependent's allowance to her, and immediately the pension of the husband was cut to $5 a month.
The point I want to make is this, that if we apply this principle to our aged and unfortunate people, and still more to the blind, and apply it to the dependents of the men in our armed forces, of restricting the amount that can be taken from the treasury, am I going too far in suggesting that the same principle should be applied where large sums of money are paid from the public treasury for other specific purposes? I have not the time in this debate to develop what I think would be a fair limit on the number of acres of summer-fallow on which a bonus is to be paid under the government's proposals, but there will be time for that later on.
I pass on to deal with the bonus of S2 an acre for seeding wheat acreage to grass. I am happy - to say that I am in full accord with that proposal. I think the members of the committee will agree with me that a vast number of acres, hundreds of thousands, yes, millions of acres in western Canada which should have been left in grass have been put under the plough. I realize also that, because of the wide acreage to be sown, the cost is great and, in addition, there is a greater weather hazard there than in other parts of Canada. Therefore we can afford to pay something out of the public treasury in an endeavour to get large areas of that country back into grass, and if we succeeded in doing that, the best thing to do would be to leave it in grass for the future.
This brings me to the third item, the proposal to pay a bonus of $2 an acre on wheat acreage that is sown to coarse grains. Of course the principle is this. It is estimated that under these proposals there will be a reduction of 9,000,000 acres in the acreage sown to wheat this year. Perhaps it is only fair that there should be some recompense for that reduction in acreage, and the bonuses that are to be paid for summer-fallowing, for sowing to grass and for sowing coarse grains, are all closely related to the 35 per cent reduction in wheat acreage.
Before ' I go further into that, in order to emphasize one point in connection with the wheat situation, I should like to refer briefly to two or three phases of the wheat marketing business in western Canada. I wish to take hon. gentlemen back to the time when

there were two joint-stock companies efficiently marketing large quantities of western grain. Those companies were in a strong financial position and accumulated large reserves, one of them, the Saskatchewan Cooperative Elevator company, building up a reserve of
811,000,000. Then some men, I am sure with an honest purpose, went through the prairies and said to the farmers, "Look at that $11,000,000 of reserves! That money should not belong to the company; it is yours, and you should have received a higher price for your wheat." Rightly or wrongly, very large numbers of farmers believed in that theory, and in that way the pool idea developed. Along with that, the idea developed that it was not necessary to have very much money to market wheat, that all one had to do was to have the wheat, pay an initial payment, and borrow money from the bank, and then when they sold the entire crop of wheat later on, they could repay any instalments still due. That was a false idea, and I am sure that western Canada has paid dearly for its experiences in that connection.
Then we come to the pool period; to the time when this organization developed a worldwide crop intelligence service which furnished not only crop reports but carefully tabulated statements of the possibilities of wheat consumption in various countries of the world. That developed in western Canada in one year the attitude of mind that wheat was worth $1.75 to $2 a bushel. Buyers came along; and when the pool and grain trade had the chance to sell large quantities of wheat at $1.40 to $1.50 a bushel, they let the opportunity pass and these world buyers went elsewhere and bought their wheat requirements at a lower price. I do not say that this was the fault of the pool or of the companies in the grain trade. Perhaps they were all equally to blame. The market in western Canada went down steadily until it fell below the initial price paid, and the banks asked, "Whose wheat is this? We have advanced more money upon it than it can be sold for", and so they stepped in and took over the wheat. That was when the wheat business began to be a real problem for the people of Canada at large.
We emerged from that period with a wheat board; and if there is any question that has been largely discussed in this chamber on previous occasions, it is the operations of the Canadian wheat board. I might recall to the committee many figures, running into $60,000,000 one year, $57,000,000 another year, and so many millions another year, but I think the committee has heard enough of that. I wish to make just this one remark. I do not

like to utter any word of criticism of those who were engaged in the various phases of marketing grain in western Canada. I am serious when I say this, that I believe their efforts were only those of honest men seeking for something better which they did not always find. I go one step further and say that when the Saskatchewan Elevator company was sold out to the pool, the guardian angel of western Canada must have been sound asleep.
There never was one.

I now come to discuss what, to my mind, is by all odds the most far-reaching item in this wheat policy. I refer to the proposal to pay a bonus of $2 an acre for the production of coarse grains. We all know that production costs of coarse grains in western Canada are less than they are in eastern Canada and other parts of the dominion. In the west they farm larger areas and produce grain cheaper; their taxes are lower, and therefore they can produce these grains for less money.
And mortgages are heavier.
What about the bonus he is getting for cheese?

I had forgotten all about that; I am glad the hon. member mentioned it. I say to hon. members: You are suggesting giving the cheese producer perhaps two, or two and a half or even three millions, if you like; I do not care. But what I want to

point out is that the cheese producers are among the largest hog producers in Ontario. If, therefore, you carry out that policy, you would put one hand in the treasury, take out money and give it to him, and then put the other hand in his pocket and take the money out again. The question of the western farmer has been brought up, and, as I said at the outset, I have great sympathy for the western Canadian farmer. Let me add that when the Minister of Trade and Commerce brings down his wheat legislation, if he will increase the 70 cents a bushel to 75 cents-[DOT]
Eighty-five.

We will discuss that suggestion later, but for the purposes of this illustration I will say 75 cents. I say, if he increases the 70 cents to 75 cents, I will rise in my place and back him up and vote for it. I say that because I think the western farmer has a problem and he must have assistance in solving it. But I do not think the solution should be to drive the farmers of Ontario and Quebec and of other parts of the dominion out of one of their strong lines of business. Most fair-minded men, I believe, will agree with me in that regard.
I may be asked, "What will the Ontario farmer do under these circumstances?" I will tell you. He will do just as he did in the last war. This nation is at war. The farmers of Ontario are as loyal as the farmers in any other part of Canada; the farmers are all loyal citizens. The farmers of Ontario, therefore, no matter what the conditions may be, will go ahead and try to the best of their ability to feed our armies at the front, the armies of our allies, and our munitions workers, and to feed all the rest of the people, they *null not lie down on the job.
My time is up and I must conclude. I maintain that if we are going to include in the agricultural policy of Canada the principle of bonusing the production of hog feed in Canada, then it must not be limited to any single area in Canada. It must be made applicable universally throughout the country. It must apply in like degree to the little farmer in the maritime provinces. The other day we saw a picture showing him ploughing the ground with a pair of horses. It must apply in like degree to the farmers in Quebec, the compatriots of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). In that province there are farmers with large hearts and larger families, and they must have a chance to live. It must apply in like degree to the farmers in Ontario, and in British Columbia where hog production is limited; and I would
say to the rest of the farmers that this legislation, as it is at present, will not help in western Canada.

No person can discuss this $35,000,000 vote to bonus wheat acreage reduction without discussing the 1941 wheat policy announced by the government on March 12, because in the final analysis this vote of $35,000,000 is compensation to make up for what the minister himself termed this afternoon the denial to the farmer of the right to sell a certain amount of his wheat.
I want first of all to commend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) for the statement he gave to the house on March 12.	It was a realistic statement.
It compares favourably with the statement given to the house on November 14 last by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) when he spoke of a five-year programme in which we will dispose of two billion bushels of wheat and find ourselves at the end of that time fifty million bushels short of actual demand. I think the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce the other day brought most of the people interested in the wheat problem down to earth. The statement was to the effect that on July 31 of this year we shall have a visible surplus of 575 million bushels; and if ail the storage facilities which are planned are finally built, we shall have only 582 million bushels of storage capacity iD Canada. In other words, by the time the wheat board has taken delivery of the 1940 crop, we shall be able this year to take into storage or take delivery of scarcely any of the 1941 wheat crop.
Any person who suggests to the government that this is an easy problem to solve is not fair either to himself or to the government. It is a tremendous problem, and we must all approach it with sympathy for the men who are charged with the responsibility of finding a solution. We must all realize that the government cannot continue to take unlimited quantities of wheat. We should realize that there must be restricted deliveries. We all realize that the farmer should not be encouraged to continue to increase his wheat acreage, but rather encouraged to curtail it. The farmers themselves have realized that; the different producers' organizations have made representations to the government. I need not review them; they were reviewed this afternoon by the Minister of Agriculture. Representations were made by the advisory committee to the wheat board, and are now on the record. Representations were made

It finally found expression in a motion brought into the Saskatchewan legislature on February 28, moved by Hon. Mr. Patterson, premier of that province, seconded by Hon. Mr. Taggart, minister of agriculture of that province. The motion read:
That this assembly request the federal government to adopt the following policy in respect to the 1941 wheat crop:
1.	That the minimum price for the 1941 wheat crop be set at 85 cents per bushel, basis No. 1 at Fort William;
2.	That a processing tax of 50 cents a bushel be levied on all wheat processed for consumption in Canada,_ the proceeds of such tax to be added to the minimum price of 85 cents a bushel;
3.	That the delivery of the 1941 crop be made on an acreage quota, such quota to be determined by the storage space available during the crop year of 1941;
4.	That the government of Canada make advances to farmers for the purpose of providing funds with which to build essential farm storage;
5.	That the government of Canada make provision for advances to farmers on the credit of the quota to be delivered;
G. That the government of Canada maintain and carry the wheat surplus as an essential part of its war policy.
This was finally passed unanimously by the entire Saskatchewan legislature. I do not for a moment suggest that this six-point wheat policy is all that I should like to see in a wheat policy, nor do I think it is all that a government could do in formulating a wheat policy. I suggest, however, that it is the irreducible minimum which western Canada can accept if western agriculture is not to receive irreparable damage.
It seems to me passing strange that, representations having been made by these different organizations, including the government of Saskatchewan, there should be brought down by this government a policy which scarcely resembles in the slightest detail the policies that have been suggested by producers' organizations. The best proof of that is that on March 14, Mr. H. H. Hannam, president for Ontario of the federation of agriculture, whose representation to the government was made on January 27, labeled it a two-barrel shotgun which would destroy both eastern and western agriculture. The wheat pools of the three prairie provinces on March 13 registered their strong disapproval of the wheat policy as announced.
What does this policy which the government has outlined mean? First of all, it does

both the things which the Minister of Agriculture suggested it did not intend to do. It brings about compulsory wheat acreage reduction. It is all very well to say that the farmer is not compelled to reduce his acreage; but, to use the minister's own words this afternoon, the farmer is denied the right to sell, and if the farmer is denied the right to sell his product, that is the most effective kind of compulsory acreage reduction. A policy of drastic acreage reduction is entirely incompatible with the rosy and optimistic picture given by the Minister of Agriculture to this house on November 14 last.
The second thing this policy does is, it pays the farmer not to grow wheat, because it does not pay him to summer-fallow, or to grow coarse grain unless the land on which he grows it is land on which he used to grow wheat. In other words, he is being paid not to grow wheat but to do something else with his land.
As I said, we realize that curtailment is necessary, that restricted delivery is necessary. But we say that the means by which the government is seeking to attain its ends are unsound and inequitable. I propose on behalf of the group with which I am associated to outline in skeleton form the six outstanding weaknesses of the government's wheat proposals, and to suggest six alternative proposals.
Our first objection is that reduction in wheat acreage is only of value if it is done in conjunction with other wheat-growing countries. Individual reduction by Canada can only help other wheat-growing countries to our detriment. If there must be acreage reduction, there should be an attempt to have the other wheat-growing nations of the world join in a concerted effort along this line. Otherwise, if this war lasts long enough, wc are simply going to push ourselves out of the wheat-growing business to the benefit of Argentina and the United States.
Our second objection is that this reduction is too drastic. While curtailment may be necessary, reduction by one-third will entail dislocation of the entire western agricultural economy. There are thousands of farmers with large investments in wheat-producing equipment which cannot overnight be adapted to other types of farming. I think every lion, member will realize that not only will there be dislocation of western agriculture but that, of necessity, there must be a dislocation of eastern agriculture. If the western farmer is to be forced to turn at least three million acres of land into the growing of coarse grains, what will happen to prices of coarse grains? Western members in this house will remember 1932, when we were selling barley

for as little as nine cents a bushel; yes, and someone says even seven cents. If prices of coarse grains drop, farmers will not sell coarse grains; they will feed them. Then next year we shall have a steady stream of hogs coming from western Canada. Previous speakers have shown already, I think, that in the last few years the hog production of Canada has trebled, and I understand that at the present moment we are shipping to Great Britain one million pounds a week over and above what is called for under our bacon agreement with the United Kingdom.
No person in this house is going to get me into a quarrel between eastern and western agriculture. I do not propose to indulge in that sort of thing. Although I represent a western constituency I, together with every other member of this house, want to look at this picture from the point of view of Canada and Canadian agricultural economy as a whole. The balance is so fine that unless we tiy to solve our western problems in a sane way, we may be only robbing Peter to pay Paul, without paying Paul very much at that. The drastic nature of this acreage reduction is shown by what will happen to the western agricultural income. I was surprised this afternoon to hear the minister speak of the wheat income for western Canada as being $178,000,000, I think he said.

The third objection to this scheme is that the price of 70 cents, basis Fort William, is altogether too low. The Minister of Agriculture has, pointed out frequently in this house that wheat can be produced most economically by farmers with two section farms, with high-powered machinery. They can produce more economically because they are on a mass-production basis; but if we reduce their acreage by one-third, their overhead will not be reduced proportionately, and their cost per unit will be proportionately higher. If these farmers could not produce wheat for 70 cents a bushel previously, certainly they cannot produce it now, with their overhead remaining stationary and the per-bushel cost increasing.
Our fourth objection to this policy is that, as it now stands, it will spell the doom of the small farmer, since the reduced acreage will increase the per-bushel cost; and no provision has been made in the proposed legislation for a maximum delivery on the first quarter-section.
Our fifth objection is that there is no provision for a cash advance even on the quota the farmer is to be allowed to deliver. According to the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the 1940 wheat crop will fill practically all the available storage space. The farmers are not likely to be able to sell any wheat until next spring or early summer. How are they going to finance from the time they take off their crops in September until they are able to sell next April or May? How are they to pay their harvesting operations? How are they to pay their store bills? How are they to keep their families throughout the winter? This committee should keep in mind the fact that the federal government has announced already to the provincial government that the federal contribution to relief is to be discontinued on March 31. What is the outlook for the farmers west of the great lakes? If no provision is made to help the farmer finance between the time he takes off his crop and the time he is allowed to deliver it, we shall see hardship in western Canada such as we have never seen before.
Our sixth objection is that the storage to be paid is only on that part of the farmer's crop which he is ultimately to be allowed to deliver. If he grows more than the quota, the government accepts no responsibility for assisting him in carrying that wheat. He is not to be allowed to sell it, but he is to be charged with the sole responsibility of carrying it. We believe that that wheat is an asset and that the government has some responsibility in connection with it, and ought to accept that responsibility by providing assistance for the farmers to enable them to carry that part of the wheat which they grow over and above what they are being permitted to sell.

I wish to place before this committee six proposals which we think ought to be accepted and incorporated into the government's wheat policy for the handling and marketing of the 1941 wheat crop. The first is that the initial price ought to be raised. It was suggested by the Saskatchewan legislature and by producers' organizations that the price be 85 cents per bushel, and that there be added to that 85 cents the proceeds from an increased processing levy. The other day the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) quoted certain statistics which had been collected by the Sirois commission on agricultural income per farm up to 1937. We have worked out the figures from the same source from 1937 to the present, and we find that during the last four years the average cash income of the farms of Canada was S472 per annum. If living in kind is added and depreciation on buildings and equipment deducted, it amounts to $632 per farm unit. In the prairie provinces the average cash income was $496, and if living in kind is added it amounts to $559. It was found that Saskatchewan had the lowest average cash income from 1937 to 1940; the average income per farm unit was $102 per annum, and when living in kind was added, it amounted to $291. These figures prove beyond any possible contradiction that an initial price of 70 cents will not meet the situation when the wheat farmer is to be allowed to deliver only 65 per cent of the wheat which he was allowed to deliver last year and the year before.
Our second proposal is that there ought to be a maximum delivery for the first quarter-section, and the quota for the remainder should be on a graduated basis. We would suggest that 1,000 or 750 bushels should be accepted for the first quarter-section and a lesser amount for each succeeding quarter-section. This would take care of the very man the minister was talking about this afternoon, the man with 100 acres in wheat, who will now have only sixty acres. He is the one who is going to feel the pinch of this most. He has no way to reduce his overhead. He is the man who ought to be allowed to make a maximum delivery from the first quarter-section.
Our third suggestion is that the government should assist the farmer to build storage facilities on his farm in order to store the surplus wheat. In the final analysis the farm is where wheat should be stored. When we realize that in 1937 this government spent $18,000,000 in buying seed grain and delivering it to the drought areas of Saskatchewan. we shall realize how important it is to have at- least 200,000,000 bushels of wheat

stored on the farms of western Canada. There could be no better crop insurance against future contingencies.
The fourth suggestion we make is that there should be a cash advance of 75 per cent of the initial price on the basis of the quota to be delivered. If a farmer knows how much wheat he is going to be allowed to deliver and the government is not in position to take delivery until next May, then the farmer should be able to get a cash advance in order to meet his outstanding obligations and carry on until such time as the government has the storage facilities to take delivery of the farmer's wheat.
Our fifth suggestion is that storage charges should be paid on wheat stored on the farm. We believe that the government has a responsibility to the farmers to assist them in carrying that part of their crops which they are not going to be permitted to sell. It will seem strange to a farmer if he is storing 2,000 bushels of wheat on his farm and can collect no storage, and a few miles down the road is an elevator full of wheat being stored for the federal government and drawing two-thirds of a cent per bushel per month for every month and every year it is there. It will be difficult to explain to a farmer why an elevator should draw storage charges and he should receive none for the wheat he is carrying against the time when this country and other parts of the world will need it.
The sixth proposal which we wish to place before this committee for its consideration is that the government should increase the processing levy on wheat milled in Canada for domestic purposes and that the proceeds of such levy should be used in assisting in financing the maximum deliveries which are to be made from the first quarter-sections.
A 50-cent processing tax would net the government about $25,000,000, which would enable the government to pay ten cents a bushel on the first 1.000 bushels to be delivered from each quarter-section. In other words, without any extra cost to the treasury the government would be enabled to pay 95 cents a bushel, if we add the 10 cents to the 85 cents proposed earlier, on the first 1,000 bushels delivered by the farmer.
I know the suggestion will be made by some hon. members that this will raise the price of bread, but I think the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) dealt with that quite adequately yesterday. The royal commission appointed in 1934 to study mass buying and price spreads found that there was no justification for raising the price of bread until the price of wheat went past $1.60 a bushel. All western members will remember that in 1938 14873-1231
the price of wheat reached $1.47 a bushel, but the price of bread did not rise. There is no reason why a 50-cent processing levy could not be placed on wheat milled for domestic consumption.

How about the small
farmer who bakes his own flour?

He should be
exempted.

Even if he were not exempted, I would point out to the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Howden) that over a period of years the price of wheat has fluctuated. When the price of wheat went down to 37 cents a bushel, the price of flour did not drop proportionately. As a matter of fact, we have in this country a milling combine which have absorbed and benefited by any drop in the price of wheat. They could afford to pay $1.35 a bushel for wheat.
That would not help out the small farmer who makes his own flour, if he has to pay a processing tax on every bushel.

It would mean at the very most one cent on one loaf, or two or three cents a day for the average family, and the average farmer would pay that gladly if he were going to get 95 cents a bushel for the first 1,000 bushels he produced.

The hon. member was
talking of farmers with $100 a year. They depend on their own flour for bread.

They would have a great deal more than $100 a year if they got 95 cents a bushel for the first 1,000 bushels they produced.
I suggest, in closing, that it seems to me that the government is halting between two opinions. The Minister of Agriculture on November 14 assured the house, and I am inclined to agree with him, that in the normal course of events world demand will absorb the huge surplus of wheat which we are likely to accumulate during the war. On the other hand the Minister of Trade and Commerce seems to be alarmed and dismayed at this growing mountain of wheat. The government seeks to alter the agricultural economy overnight and to turn one-third of the wheat-producing lands in western Canada into the production of coarse grains or into summer-fallow. which in the final analysis will produce still more wheat.
While we realize that the expansion of wheat acreage at this time is most undesirable and that a certain amount of curtailment may be necessary, we deprecate most vigorously so drastic a reduction in -wheat acreage. The prairie provinces in general, and Saskatchewan

Supply-Agriculture-Wheat Acreages
in particular, by reason of their climate and topography, are ideally situated for the growing of wheat. Large areas of the prairies are ill suited for any other kind of farming. We still grow the finest wheat in the world, and when this war is over there will be starving millions to be fed, not only in Europe but in Asia, where a unified and victorious China may open up markets larger than any of which we have ever dreamed. We must not lose our vision at this time. We must not allow the temporary problems contingent upon the war to distort the long-term view. What guarantee have we that nature will continue to give us the great wheat crops that we have had in the past two years? A few years ago certain people of western Canada said, "If only we had a crop, all would be well." Now they say, "If only we did not have a crop, all would be well." What is 500 million bushels of wheat? Two or three complete crop failures would find the grain bins of western Canada empty again. The Saskatchewan members of this house will remember as I do a time, not very long ago, when some of the prairie farmers were burning their straw stacks, and within two years those same farmers were scouring the prairies looking for straw to keep their stock alive.
Have we forgotten the lesson of Joseph, who during the bountiful years in Egypt built vast granaries and stored huge quantities of wheat and corn? He was wise in his day and generation, and the monument to his memory is contained in those simple words, that when the famine came, "there was corn in Egypt." Let it not be said of us that we had less foresight than Joseph.
Therefore it seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that the task of this government is twofold: first, to prevent any increase in wheat acreage, and, if necessary, to encourage curtailment; and. second, in the manner in which I have outlined, to make it possible for wheat producers to get a fair price for a part of their crop and to be given assistance in carrying the remainder of their crop against that day when returning peace and the free exchange of world commodities will declare to the world once again that "wheat is king."

In rising to take part in this debate to-night, I am going to take a rather different attitude from that of some previous speakers, in that I intend to give this government some praise for what they have done for agriculture. I believe that the government are to be commended for the legislation which they have brought down to benefit the farmers, not only of the west but of all Canada. The name of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has been prominently before the people of late, and I believe that we have in the present minister as fine a Minister of Agriculture as Canada ever had. He knows the problems of the farmers of Canada as well as, and perhaps better than, any other man we could get. We may not all agree with what he says and what he does, but we appreciate the position which he is in to-day, and we know that, in the main, he is doing a really good job.
Since I came to the house six years ago, I have tried on several occasions to place before parliament the condition of the farmer in Canada, and perhaps more particularly the position of the farmer of Ontario. I have tried to show the difference between his costs of production and what he really receives for his product, which, after all, is the main problem as far as the farmer is concerned. It is not so important to consider what the farmer receives for his produce as what it costs him to produce it. I believe I am safe in saying that 75 per cent of the farmers of Ontario would be satisfied with the prevailing prices
for their products if costs of production correspond with what they receive. But the history of agriculture shows that always in time of war when the agriculturist produces a surplus of goods, he experiences great difficulty in selling them, particularly in the early stages of the war. That was true of the last war and it is true of the present one. As the last war progressed, prices rose, perhaps to a height which they should not have reached. I hope the same thing does not happen again, because I believe it was one of the worst things that ever occurred so far as agriculture was concerned.
To-day all industrial activity in Canada continues to increase with the expansion of war demand. There is an increase of employment and of non-agricultural income. According to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), our expenditure on the prosecution of the war for the year commencing April 1, 1941, will amount to approximately $1,460,000,000, the largest, sum which was ever voted by any parliament in Canada. Included in this sum is an item of $177,928,000 for the expansion of industry, which indicates that the productive capacity of Canadian industry will be substantially increased, and therefore should lead to an enlargement of domestic demand.
Since June, 1940, the continuous rise of wholesale prices has been inevitable. All commodities have risen to some extent, and for the month of February averaged 84-6 of 1926 as compared with 82-8 the previous year. Prices of farm produce have also risen slightly but have not yet made up the loss sustained in the early part of 1940. This may be due in large measure to the low price of wheat. All live stock registered some strength in February, and should continue to show gains as the domestic demand increases.
I have here an index of living costs on the 1935-39 basis; they rose from 108-0 in the month of December to 108-3 in January, 1941, but the general index in the year from January to January was 108-3 this year, compared with 103-8 in January, 1940, showing that the cost of living increased by 5 per cent.
At the present time exportation of agricultural products is difficult because of the uncertainty in the supply of Shipping. To-day the bulk of Canada's exports goes either to the United Kingdom or to the United States. We have heard a great deal of discussion of late from some hon, members of the opposition about what this government has or has not done for the relief of the farmer. I believe that the hon. member for Huron North stated last November, referring to the farmers, "We never did get a fair deal from any government, least of all from this one." The hon.

We all know that the price of cattle in 1941 on the Toronto market has been anywhere from $8.50 to $9.50 and as high as $10. In the case of lamb, prices are somewhat lower. We might go back to 1926. as some have done, and take it on the basis of 1926-29. I could give prices of cheese, milk and eggs and of many other farm products, but those three are enough to allow a comparison of prices as between 1930-35 and 1935-40. We owe a great deal to this government and particularly to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) for the agreement he made with the United States whereby we sell our cattle in that market. We are getting the best price for beef cattle that we have had in many years. We are selling all our surplus cattle to the United States, and I believe that up to date it has not been necessary to send any cattle to Great Britain as part of the war effort. The United States is taking all our cattle and will take more if it can get them.
We have heard the suggestion that the price of farm products should be put on the basis of 1926-29, but so far as cattle are concerned I believe we have had, in 1941, a price well above that figure. Of course, in one dairy industry, cheese constitutes one of the chief products, and we are selling to Great Britain at a price of 14-4 cents all the cheese we can produce. This government is adding another 3/5ths of a cent, making it fifteen cents, with a bonus of S2 on 94 score cheese and $1 on 93, and the province of Ontario is giving a bonus of two cents, making the cheese price in Ontario to-day nineteen cents, f.o.b. Montreal on best grade. In my opinion the producer of cheese can 
produce at that price. We have a contract with Great Britain for 112,000,000 pounds, and I think we should be able to supply that quantity at the price offering.
Then there is the butter situation. We have heard a good deal of discussion of price pegging, the setting of a minimum price. Perhaps the butter situation did give rise to a lot of discussion and may have started the whole story, but I do not think the government made any great mistake in setting the price. I could never see why speculators should buy 60,000,000 pounds from the farmers at twenty-one cents a pound and be allowed to sell it to the consumer at forty and forty-two cents. But that is what was taking place. I believe that if the price board would set a minimum price which would be reasonable to the farmer for the summer, the producer of butter would be much better off than if he took the market price of twenty or twenty-one cents, such as obtained last summer, and obtained forty-two cents in the winter.
Then there is the hog situation, about which there has been considerable discussion. We have an agreement with Great Britain. Someone has suggested that we should send bacon to Great Britain free. Others think that we are not getting enough and should take the price Great Britain is paying us and the government subsidize to the 1926-29 level. We have promised to supply Great Britain with 420,000,000 pounds of bacon, and since that contract was entered into, we have been producing an average of 3,000,000 pounds of bacon a week in excess of the contract. Great Britain has agreed to take
1,000,000 pounds a week more than the contract, which means that to-day we are storing in our cold storage plants 2,000,000 pounds a week. I wonder sometimes, if the price of bacon were raised to the 1926-29 level, what we would do. I imagine we would have more hogs ten times over than we could sell. History proves that the minute you make anything really profitable for the grower, you get too much of it.
A word about the apple situation. I am interested in apples, and I believe that the apple growers of Canada are more than satisfied with the assistance given them by this government. I do not think any member of the house will contradict that statement. We have sold our apples at a reasonable price because we have received protection from this government.
I come now to one of the most important items of legislation, namely, the wheat problem. Some days ago the Minister of Agriculture gave a summary of the situation.

He announced the policy with regard to wheat, whereby wheat deliveries are to be taken up to 230,000,000 bushels at a price of 70 cents, basis Fort William No. 1 northern. This will mean considerably less income for the western farmer; there is no doubt about that. But to offset the acreage being taken out of wheat, it is proposed that $4 an acre be paid for summer-fallow, S2 an acre for sowing to grass seed, and $2 an acre for coarse grain. The idea is to reduce wheat acreage by 9,000,000 acres. We in Ontario have been and still are willing to help the western farmer, and for a period of years we have paid our share of the many millions of dollars contributed towards the assistance of the west. We are still willing to do that; but we do feel that the bonusing of coarse grain, particularly bonusing, to the extent of S2 an acre, the western farmer to grow coarse grain, is going a step too far.
I am not so much opposed to summer-fallow, although I do not believe that is the right thing to do either. I think, as far as grass seeding is concerned, that is something which should be encouraged. We have broken up too much land in the west for the growing of wheat, and it would be a good idea to get it seeded back. I would be more willing to pay $4 an acre to seed down than $4 an acre for summer-fallow or $2 an acre for coarse grain. I am afraid we shall be establishing a precedent of fixing a price on coarse grains just as we have on wheat. As the hon. member for Victoria, Ontario, said, I would rather pay a little higher price for wheat, perhaps 72 or 75 cents, and stick to wheat, than bonus the growing of coarse grains to come into competition with the eastern farmers, which to my mind must happen; I cannot see anything else for it. The amount itself may not be so great but the principle of the thing seems to me absolutely wrong.
As far as this proposal is concerned I as an Ontario farmer do not feel that I can support it, especially if this coarse grain clause is left in. I hope the government will consider this seriously and for the sake of the hog producer and the grain grower in Ontario leave this clause out. If that were taken out, I believe we could explain to our people the reason why it is of advantage to bonus summer-fallow and grass seeding. We realize fully that we have too much wheat. Some land must be taken out of wheat and put into something else. We expect in 1941 a surplus of wheat of between eight and nine hundred million bushels, although the world surplus of wheat is expected to be 1,500 million bushels. Someone said wheat is a war casualty, but I do not agree with that; we had too much
*wheat before the war started, and if in the years from 1935 on we had had big crops, we would have had ten times more wheat than we can sell.
As I said, labour to-day has a guarantee of the scale of wages of 1926-29 plus an increase for the rise in the cost of living. I am not complaining about that, but surely what is good for one is good for another. The cost of production of the farmer has risen considerably; that is one of the reasons why I have to take this attitude. Take our farm implements; the price of a six-foot binder to-day is $240; when I started farming I bought a six-foot binder complete for $120. About three companies control the price of farm implements. It does not seem to make any difference how much the duty is reduced, the price continues to rise. The duty was 25 per cent; it was reduced to 7| per cent, and the price went up.
Then there is the scarcity of help, especially as far as the dairy farmer is concerned. Some argue that taking men from the farms does not make any difference to the farmer, that the farming industry will remain intact. But anyone who is in the dairy business to-day depends absolutely on hired help, and if his man goes to the city and gets a job at anywhere from $100 to $125 for two weeks' work, as they have done, the industry is bound to suffer.
Over a period of years Canadian manufacturing industry has been protected by all governments, perhaps beyond what it should be. I am not a free trader; I believe in a certain amount of protection, but I believe that by protecting industry with a high tariff we are doing a great injustice to the farmers. I have noticed, since coming to this house, several hon. members of the opposition have made many pleas for the farmer, but every time protection for industry comes up they are right on the job. We must be consistent; we must be reasonable.
We have to-day in Canada what is known as the federation of agriculture. We have in organizations of one kind and another 350,000 farmers, or practically half the farmers of this dominion. We have 340 farm organizations selling to the farmer, and over 320 farm organizations that buy from the farmer. I am all in sympathy with farm organizations; farmers have a right to make their requests known to any government. Farmers have not enough representation in this House of Commons. I took the trouble the other day to go over the book and I found that there are about thirty-five farmers in the house. We have some others who are classed as farmers, gentlemen farmers; we are glad to have them; they are an asset to our industry, but of

real honest-to-goodness farmers who know what it means to do a real day's work on a farm, we have about thirty-five.
Farm organizations and federations of agriculture can do a great job for the farmers if they are reasonable in their requests. But if they are going to demand the impossible, the organizations will not be of much help. It is all very well to be critical, but we must offer something constructive if we are going to get anywhere. Representations have been made to this government by farm organizations, and as the Minister of Agriculture said their ideas in many instances have been accepted and put into effect by the government. If they continue to do this in a businesslike way, I believe the farmers of this country will eventually get a better deal.

Like the previous speaker, I hesitate to criticize this government too much. I passed through the trying times we had under different governments, and it gives me a cold chill to think I might do anything to injure the government we have now. That resolution, and a vote of lack of confidence in this government from an hon. member who sat under the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett when we as farmers were hiring help and paying our men from pigs at three cents a pound-in fact, I sold the last batch at 2.90-from cattle at three cents a pound, while the honoured present leader of the opposition sat smiling at the pleasant times the farmers were having! I was in extreme distress at that time; I had five hundred acres; I went home in cold sweat and sold every acre of land I had and got out of it. I put my sheep, cattle and horses out on shares. I waited and I bought the land back later at half the price. I sold these farms to organizers who believed what the Conservatives were telling them about butter. They got in their cows; butter was thirty cents, and they were told by the Conservative party, "No more butter at thirty cents." And there was not until the Liberals came into power. These men came and asked me to take back the farms off their hands. I said I was sorry, but I had made other arrangements; I had other ideas.
Doctor, you are a financier.

I have again five hundred acres, and I am going to hold them until this government is defeated. I am going to hold out; but if ever this government is defeated, I will part with that land just as quickly as I can, get rid of it.
I hope the government will not pay too much attention to the far corner or to the

western members. We hear a great deal of nonsense in this chamber. We have a member who comes from Qu'Appelle, who rises in his place and shadow-boxes with the Liberals on the other side. They are all planning together how to get a little bite out of the government, how to get a little donation. I have watched that go on time and again, and I have said to myself, "More shadow-boxing." Here the hon. member rises in his place and speaks as though he is opposed to this scheme, but really he is tickled to death to see the amount of money that is going to the west. But let us not give the west everything they ask. I can see the difficulty the minister has; no matter what you give them you can never satisfy them.
Is this Canadian unity?

Say, listen, down in that comer; we have people from the west appealing to the ministers to build chimneys on schoolhouses, to clean children's heads and all such nonsense as that. Now we are beginning to bonus them. This is against the fundamental principles of the Liberal party. I believe if the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett were here to-day, he would blush to see some of the things we are putting through. We have gone further than the Tories would go. We are destroying the Liberal party. We are giving away too much. We are beginning to give bonuses and subsidies, and we are finding white elephants left on our hands.
Look at the wheat problem; it is our own fault. The western farmers pleaded and pleaded, and now they have a baby elephant on their hands and do not know what to do with it. Neither does the minister know what to do with it. Now they want a bonus on coarse grains, and we have to pay the farmer for storing his grain. Why, if I were a western farmer and were paid eight cents for storing my wheat, I would build a great big barn and keep wheat for centuries. They are getting eleven per cent and more on their money, and now that you are going to give bonuses and subsidies you should cut that down. Why, if they got two or three cents, that would be plenty. I never let a tramp ask for a dinner in vain, but I never gave him a very fat dinner. Charity should be fairly well circumscribed, and when the west comes to the minister asking for donations to this and that, he should give them very little. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle and the other members from the west fight against this or that, and ask for the other thing, but they all agree when they get to their offices upstairs.

We have done so much for the west. There is the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. That act was to be in force only until the farmers got on their feet again; but we find that even this year, when they have so much grain they do not know what to do with it, they still have this act. When are they going to be rehabilitated? If they are not rehabilitated now, when will they be? Then we have the Prairie Farm Assistance Act; the reestablishment of settlers; direct relief; material aid; feed and fodder; shipment of live stock, and so on, each costing millions of dollars. Saskatchewan seems to get the biggest share of the boodle, 856,772.000 altogether. Alberta gets only $7,565,000 and Manitoba only $2,438,000.
There may be something in it when they appeal to us to bonus them in the name of charity. When they cannot sell their wheat they have a right to some consideration, and I think they should get it, but I am afraid the minister will go too far if he does what he has suggested. According to the Sirois report-which is strongly condemned in Ontario but appears to be all right nationally-we find that the individual income in Prince Edward Island was $221. In Alberta it was $360, which meant that in Alberta the individual had an advantage of $139 over the individual in Prince Edward Island; and still the people of the west are asking for more. The individual in Saskatchewan had an advantage of $40, and the individual in Manitoba an advantage of $166 over the individual in Prince Edward Island1; still they aTe asking for more. I suppose these herrings down on the coast can live for less, but in any event they are not here asking for donations.

What about
Ontario?

I think it is a great mistake to loosen the purse-strings too much in giving these subsidies. I do not believe there is a western farmer here who will not boast that the west can run Ontario off the map in growing pigs. I could name dozens of hon. members who have made that statement. I say to them, grow your grain and feed your pigs. We will take a chance on being run off the map, but do not ask Ontario farmers to pay you to grow the grain. We do not object to meeting you on an equal basis, but I am sure our farmers will object if you ask them to pay you $2 an acre to grow coarse grains to feed pigs which you will sell in competition- with those raised in Ontario. Remember, the Ontario farmer must pay a good part of that $2. I think you are overdoing it, and I hope there will be some modification, especially in
connection with coarse grains. The rate for summeT-fallow is too high, also. It does not take $4 an acre to summer-fallow in the west; you can do it for a good deal less than that. The -people of the west are getting much more than the people of the maritimes; yet they are asking for charity. I believe they should be given a certain amount, but I hope the minister will keep that amount within strict limits so that our Ontario farmers will not object too seriously.
I must say that the minister and the government have done splendid work; I think the butter question was handled particularly well. It was all right to put a reasonable peg on the top price of butter, but I hope the minister will also put a peg on the bottom price. The distance between the floor and the ceiling is the measure of what the speculators and the packers get in -profits. If the minister wants to compensate Ontario to some extent for this subsidy on coarse grains, which will mean that the farmers of Ontario will pay the farmers of the west to raise pigs in competition with them, that might be done by pegging the minimum price of butter at a reasonable level. In passing, may I say that I hope the minister will limit the amount of land on which the bonus may be paid. A man who has five or six thousand acres is not a subject of charity. If the government is to pay for storing grain in granaries there should be some limit upon the amount to be stored. If we keep a thousand bushels from one winter to the next, that is our business. We generally do it because we think it will be profitable.
Some western farmers operate farms of from five to six thousand acres. Are we going to bonus all these men? If I had a farm that size, I would summer-fallow the whole thing. There should be some limitation. I know the acreage in wheat in the previous year will guide to a certain extent the amount of bonus to be paid, but at the same time I would modify the payments. I would keep them down in order that we might appease our eastern farmers.

The hon. member for Durham (Mr. Rickard) referred to the fact that when the tariff on farm implements was lowered, the price went up. My hon. friends will recall quite readily the time when the statements from the Liberal side were entirely different from what we are hearing to-day. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) said that the members of the government were whole-heartedly in accord with this movement, and it must be alarming for him to hear two of his followers be critical of it.

I believe, however, that no one can view the agricultural situation of this country without being greatly alarmed.
For many years the agriculturist of this country has received much less than his just share of the national income. From 1926 to 1930 over 30 per cent of our people were engaged directly in agriculture. The farmer's income was only eighteen per cent of the national income, even though thirty per cent of our people were engaged in agriculture. For the last seven years over thirty per cent of our people have been engaged in agriculture, but they have received only eight per cent of the national income. The average income of 730,000 farmers of Canada has been $8 a week per family. The father, mother, and the boys and girls labour from early morning until late at night to make an income equal to the minimum price provided by statute for the office girl in the city.
Our industrialists are given cost plus ten per cent contracts. The labouring men of this country have, by statute, been guaranteed a reasonable wage. The farmer, however, is operating on a cost-minus basis. The dairyman is given a maximum price for his butter. The hon. member for Wellington North (Mr. Blair) said that he would support it if the price was put on the other end, although I believe he said he would support it anyway. He thought there should be a floor as well as a ceiling. The hog producer has been given the special privilege of producing more for less. It is not much wonder that the farmer feels that he is a "loss leader" in this new modern society in which only those who organize and demand, receive a just reward for their individual efforts. The federation of agriculture, which met in Toronto not long ago, put this pretty well in the words of Mr. Hannam when he said:
In the seventeenth month of the war we are so sincerely worried and alarmed about the detrimental effect which the present trend of national policies is inflicting upon agriculture that we deem it our duty to so advise our people and our national leaders in the hope that adjustments may be made before the unity of our people is affected and before our war effort suffers a setback.
This problem affects a great mass of our people. It has been my privilege to observe the general tendency of agricultural development in this country over many years. I have been a member of this house for some time, and there are hon. members that have been here longer than I, but it is in no spirit of "I told you so" that I remind the committee that in 1926, 1927, and especially in 1928, I stated

that we were developing a lop-sided agriculture. The hon. member from the other province nods his head. He was here at that time.
He said 1932.

Nineteen thirty-two as well.
But that statement had no influence upon many people. It was only a few of us from the old provinces of Quebec and Ontario who felt that way. The hon. member for Wey-burn (Mr. Douglas) made an excellent speech this evening, and like him I do not for one moment want to raise an issue as between the east and the west, or refer to the advantages which the east may have and which the west has not, or which the west may have and the east has not. However, coming from Ontario, I think it is only fair to state that the old provinces of Quebec and Ontario produced more gross agricultural wealth in 1938 than all the rest of the provinces combined. This is the information contained in the year book, and I think it will be found in almost every year since that time. I make this statement with all due respect to that great granary and bread-basket, the province of Saskatchewan.
I have been impressed with the grasp which hon. members have of this problem, and I have been pleased with their reference to the need of diversification of production. I well recall having stated in this house in 1928 that we would soon find the great west filled with unsold wheat. An hon. member who then sat to my left met me aftenvards in the lobby and told me that while I might know about conditions in Ontario, I knew nothing about conditions in the west. He told me they would never sell wheat for less than $1 a bushel, that they would grow wheat and wheat alone as long as they were in agriculture. I only wish to point out what I have urged before-
Oh, oh.

My hon. friend laughs, but
he is still of the same mind. He is a member of the same order. I would remind him of what one of his colleagues said to-night. We were told that if the duty on farm implements were reduced, we would be able to buy them cheaper, but we had to pay more. I can well recall that in 1932, as the hon. member has said, I contended, as I contend to-night, that if in an effort to find a sound solution for this problem, it was thought wise to maintain a board of grain commissioners, we should also establish a board of live stock commissioners. This is necessary if we are going to have a properly diversified agriculture. In 1932 I

urged upon the government of the day, which I was supporting, the establishment of an export marketing board which would administer the bonusing of live stock exports of a high quality and study the markets of the world.
Let me recall to the committee that in 1921 the value of our live stock production was greater than our grain production, yet we lost those markets. By 1930 we imported
40,000,000 pounds of meat and 55,000,000 pounds of butter to feed our people. Some are fearful that we are going to have too much animal fats. If the government is going to turn some of this wheat into the production of animal fats and if it is fearful there will be too much, why should they object to tariff board reference No. 99? Why not impose a tax of three cents a pound on vegetable shortening and two cents a pound on the vegetable oil content of soap? That would bring four or five million dollars into the treasury-and heaven knows it needs it-[DOT] and it would mean seven or eight million dollars for the farmers of this country. This suggestion is in keeping with what I have advocated on many occasions.
We have witnessed the government going into the wheat business, and to-night we see a monument to their clumsy mismanagement of this business down through the years. We have on hand millions of bushels of wheat which we cannot sell and which we might have used in the production of other products, and now to-night the government proposes a restriction of the wheat acreage. All through the years this government has been in power we have been passing estimates for scientific research, experimental work, and other means of increasing agricultural production. In other words, we have had one arm of the Department of Agriculture spending huge sums on experiment and research to increase production, and now it is proposed at greater expense to create another arm to restrict production.
Bonuses have been considered in the past, Mr. Chairman, by hon. members to your right and by many to your left. Bonuses and subsidies have been termed vicious. I urged bonuses ten years ago to encourage the development of mixed farming products in order that we might diversify our agricultural production. Since that time we have seen the government bonus products of which there were huge unsold surpluses. Now we have this government bonusing men to do nothing, to restrict the acreage of wheat. We have now a government policy of not to grow wheat, a policy that is going to cost this country $35,000,000, after we have witnessed this government going into the wheat business, and at a cost of $100,000,000 bonusing producers and building storage capacity for unsold surpluses. If a bonus policy ever was vicious, surely it is vicious now to bonus men to do nothing when Great Britain is fighting with her back to the wall. As someone has neatly said to-night-and I thought it was a good joke-in fifteen years the boys will come back from overseas, and we can picture one of them asking his father in Canada, "What were you doing while I was fighting?" and his daddy farmer replies, "Well, son, I was summer-fallowing."
In the days to come it will be infinitely better that we should have too much of foodstuffs on hand than not enough. It is bad psychologjr to restrict the production of wheat at a time when the government is urging everyone else to produce. It seems to me an unwise and unsound policy, and certainly it is not doing what the government of Great Britain is urging us to do.
I shall be glad to support anything that will help the western grain growers because I realize they are faced with a serious problem, and I know the Minister of Agriculture is struggling with it desperately at the present time. He is generally recognized, I think, as one of the most skilful political pilots we have seen in this house for a long time, but may I suggest that so far as agriculture is concerned he has clumsily driven it into the most hazardous tailspin it has experienced in the last fifteen years.
Not long ago in the British House of Commons that greatest of modem statesmen, the Prime Minister, the Right Hon. Winston Churchill, said:
We shall do our best to encourage the building up of reserves of food all over the world, so that there will always be held before the eyes of the people of Europe, including-I say this deliberately-the German and Austrian peoples, the certainty that the shattering of nazi power will bring them all immediate food, freedom and peace.
In view of that ringing challenge for our assistance in building up reserves of food, I am not surprised that the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce should bring down this policy to restrict production as a joint measure of the two ministers, because I do not think there is a member of the government who would have the courage to bring down this fantastic proposal and father such a child alone. The policy proposed here is the very opposite of what we are being urged to do by the British government. The United States of America are going to export $450,000,000 worth of agricultural products, and yet only a short time ago they were destroying their hogs and

burning their cotton in the south. Now it is in demand for the manufacture of cordite and other explosives.
The Minister of Agriculture said this afternoon that a few years ago we had only 28 million bushels of wheat in this country. If we have another drought year, and if this war should be over in a comparatively short period, is it not better for us to build up reserves of food which will surely be required after the war is over? What is 500 million bushels of wheat distributed throughout the world?
Swiftly changing and tragic events have created new problems. To-day while we grimly face a dark and difficult future, we have faith in our strength to restore peace through victory. The restoration of the agricultural industry is vital to Canada's economic fabric, to enable us to withstand the financial obligations which the war imposes; but if we are to justify our place in the life of the empire, we must answer the call of Britain and have available large stores of food for a hungry and starving world if peace should happily come sooner than we expect. When that day comes-and we all pray to God it may be soon-when peace dawns once again and world rehabilitation stands as the next gigantic Anglo-American task, we dhall surely find more opportunity to give our bonused surpluses to the poverty and hunger-stricken peoples throughout the world than to boast of higher temporary prices established by this fantastic plan to curtail production. I say this in all sincerity. I do not wish to embarrass the government, at all, not so much as some hon. members may wish to do before this issue is closed, but I do urge the government to reconsider bonusing any industry in Canada for doing nothing. I appeal to the minister to consider the matter again. I would rather spend $100,000,000 or even $200,000,000 to send foodstuffs to Great Britain than pay half that amount to men in this country to do nothing.
Why not encourage agriculture to produce more? Why not put a bonus on cheese and bacon? I may be asked: "Where would you sell it?" I reply that there are thousands of women and children crying for these products to-day, and if this war is over in two years, all the foodstuffs we can produce will be required. But this policy of restricting production, as the hon. member for Weyburn said to-night, is a long way from the policy which Joseph followed in Egypt of accumulating stores of food against the day of famine when they would be needed.
Are hon. gentlemen opposite prepared to say to Mr. Churchill, "We did not do what you asked us to do. We did not build up reserves of our No. 1 hard wheat, but, instead,

we paid our farmers for doing nothing, and we are going to get their votes because we shall get higher prices for their products when they are needed so badly after the war is over."
I say again, Mr. Chairman, I shall be glad to support any policy that wall really help to solve the great problem of agriculture, but I maintain that this policy will not solve it. This solution will only create another agriculture problem in eastern Canada. I have much regal'd for the wheat producers, and by the way I produce quite a bit myself, but wheat is not our only agricultural product. The live stock industry has produced great wealth for Canada, and you do not have to produce much live stock before you add to the richness of the soil; but when you produce wheat, you deplete the fertility of the soil. So far as cash returns are concerned, the provinces of Ontario and Quebec have, in the last ten years, produced more agricultural wealth than the rest of Canada combined.
May I remind hon. gentlemen that after the last war we shipped 77 million pounds of live stock products to Great Britain before 1921. This is a different war, it is -true, but after this war the people will be just as hungry as they were after the first great war. and where are they going to find the foodstuffs they will need? I urge the minister to reconsider whether this policy of restriction of production is sound or unsound in the interests of the empire. We must wrin the victory, and I have never known any country to lose victory because it had too large a surplus of food.
